title: What If School Integration Isn’t The Key To Education Equity?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler questions the common assumption that school integration is the main lever for improving outcomes for Black and low-income students. She reviews competing studies of 1970s and 1980s integration, notes that those data are over forty years old, and points out that integrated schools can still be internally segregated by tracking and leveled reading. She also challenges the claim that disadvantaged students simply get less money, citing recent studies showing that average per-pupil funding is not lower for poor and Black students, and that high spending in Washington, D.C. has not produced strong reading results. Her own conclusion is that what is taught and how it is delivered matters most, because weak early reading instruction and thin content knowledge leave students without family advantages behind. She grants integration may bring benefits but argues it is neither necessary nor sufficient for equity.
points: The evidence on integration is mixed and dated, and it is hard to separate family background from what the school itself contributes.
Integrating a school does not integrate its classrooms, since tracking and ability grouping, including leveled reading, can recreate segregation inside the building.

Recent funding studies suggest disadvantaged students now receive as much or more money on average, and D.C.'s high spending alongside low reading proficiency shows money alone does not raise outcomes.
Wexler locates the real equity lever in curriculum, specifically systematic phonics and content-rich instruction that builds knowledge and vocabulary for children who do not get it at home.
She suggests researchers study the scattered schools and districts that have switched to knowledge-building curricula before concluding that nothing works in high-poverty settings.
quotes: A North Carolina study found that segregation within schools, often known as tracking, accounted for up to 40% of all racial segregation in the state, and it was more common in counties with more integration at the school level. The study also said tracking was more common at higher grade levels.

A third recent study found that more funding goes to Black students than white ones, as well as to poorer kids as compared to wealthier ones. Disadvantaged students also have more full-time teachers and smaller class sizes, although they’re more likely to have inexperienced teachers.
Predominantly Black schools certainly used to get less funding than whiter schools, and some still do. But on average, that no longer seems to be the case.
And yet only 23% of D.C. eighth-graders score at the proficient level or above on national reading tests, nine percentage points below the national average. Racial and income-based gaps are huge.

Children who have access to that knowledge at home, because their parents have more education, end up further advantaged as a result. And teacher-training programs routinely inculcate beliefs that conflict with scientific findings on how kids learn. The kids who still manage to learn are generally those whose families are in a better position to support them.

Well-integrated schools undoubtedly bring benefits, and I hope we have them someday. But integration isn’t necessary to improve education for students from historically marginalized communities and low-income families, nor would it be enough.
